processing: A pan-fired green. The historic method ran through plucking, sorting, withering, pan-firing to fix the leaf, rolling, roasting and a final fine sort.
harvest_season: Spring, as usual for Anhui greens; little is documented on the exact picking dates of the modern tea.
appearance_dry: Twisted green strands, as is usual for a pan-fired Huizhou green.
appearance_liquor: Clear yellow-green, as is typical of pan-fired Huizhou greens.
appearance_wet: Even green leaf, as is usual for this type.
taste_profile: Little is documented about the modern tea's taste. Expect a fuller, more roasted-edged cup than a baked green, as with other pan-fired teas of the region; nobody knows how the original tasted.

brewing.notes: As with other pan-fired greens, it takes slightly hotter water than a bud tea. Shorten the steeps if it turns sharp.

vintage_note: As with other Anhui greens, it is sold as the current spring's harvest and is best drunk within about a year. The historic name does not mean an old tea: what you buy is a fresh, modern green from Xiuning.
description:
Songluo is less a famous drink today than a famous idea. It comes from Songluo Shan in Xiuning county, in the old Huizhou region of southern Anhui, and it is remembered as one of the teas that defined pan-fired green tea in the Ming.

The method attributed to it goes pick, sort, wither, pan-fire, roll, roast, then sort again. That sequence reads like a blueprint for loose-leaf tea as we know it, and it is often credited as a source for later teas of the area.

Few describe its taste in detail, so go in expecting a fuller pan-fired green rather than a delicate bud tea.

Buy the current spring from a seller who can name Xiuning. This is one to try for curiosity and history, side by side with Tunxi green, which is said to have grown out of it.
history:
Songluo was famous by the Ming, when pan-firing had replaced steaming. Tradition credits the method to a monk living on the Songluo mountains, with no name reliably attached.

Tunxi green, a major export style from Huizhou, is said to have developed from refined Songluo in the Qing reigns of Jiaqing and Daoguang.
